content.intro: This lesson covers When to Return an Error and When to Panic. It sits in Module 10, Error Handling, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: When to Return an Error and When to Panic matters when you work with explicit absence and failure paths. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A panic signals that the current operation cannot continue normally. Use Result for expected failures callers may handle, and reserve panics for broken assumptions or unrecoverable situations.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For When to Return an Error and When to Panic, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Expected failures should normally be represented by Result. Use ? only in a function whose return type can represent the propagated error.
